_comment: Customer-facing copy for ideas written before the routine produced its own `public` block (2026-11-02). Keyed by idea id (date-n). An idea's own `public` field in its day file wins. Shown on the public site; see build.js.

2026-10-21-1.summary: Short oral checks on each student's own code, so you can tell who understands what they submitted without spending 30 hours on oral exams.
2026-10-21-1.problem: You get polished code from students who cannot explain it. Oral exams work, but for a large class they take days of staff time, and general AI quiz tools ask about the topic, not about the lines the student actually wrote.
2026-10-21-1.forWhom: Instructors and TAs of programming courses with 60 to 400 students.
benefits: Every student gets questions about their own functions, names and commits
Students answer in a timed session from a link, no account needed
Suggested scores with quotes from the answers, for you to approve
A short list of the students who need a real conversation

2026-10-21-2.summary: Upload your slides and Jupyter notebooks and get reviewed alt text for every code screenshot, chart and diagram, written into the files for you.
2026-10-21-2.problem: Accessibility rules now require alt text on course materials, and campus services will fix your PDFs but will not write it for you. Computing slides are full of code screenshots, trees and plots, and writing hundreds of useful descriptions by hand takes weeks.
2026-10-21-2.forWhom: Computing and data science instructors who own their slides and notebooks.
benefits: A list of every image that is missing alt text
Suggested descriptions that say what a student needs to know about each image
Code screenshots turned into real, readable code
Fixed files back, plus a report for each course

2026-10-21-3.summary: Fresh practice questions for AP Computer Science Principles, written about each student's own project code.
2026-10-21-3.problem: The AP exam asks students about the code in their own project, but there are only a few official practice sets. Writing personal practice questions for 30 different student programs is more than any teacher has time for.
2026-10-21-3.forWhom: High school AP Computer Science Principles teachers, often the only CS teacher in their school.
benefits: Unlimited practice question sets for each student's project
An answer checklist for every question
A check that each project has the parts the exam requires
Printable packets for timed practice in class

2026-10-22-1.summary: See which of your graders are harsher or more lenient than the rest, before grades go out.
2026-10-22-1.problem: When several TAs split hundreds of submissions, students get different grades for the same work depending on who graded them. Most instructors only find out from regrade requests, and nobody has time to run the numbers mid-semester.
2026-10-22-1.forWhom: Instructors and head TAs of large courses with three or more graders per assignment.
benefits: Upload a grading export and get results in minutes
See each grader's harshness, and which rubric items they apply differently
A list of the questions that need a second look
A one-page summary for your TA meeting

2026-10-22-2.summary: If you allow coding assistants like Claude Code in your course, see how each student actually used them.
2026-10-22-2.problem: When students may use an AI coding assistant, the code alone does not show who made the decisions. Reading every student's full assistant session is impossible, so you cannot tell good use from blind copying.
2026-10-22-2.forWhom: University instructors and TAs in project and software engineering courses that allow AI coding tools.
benefits: Students hand in their assistant sessions with their code, with private details removed
A short summary for each student of what the assistant did and what they changed
Flags for students who accepted everything without checking
Works with GitHub-based courses and Canvas

2026-10-22-3.summary: Recommendation letter requests in one place: a request form with the student's details and consent, a deadline tracker, and notes you kept on each student.
2026-10-22-3.problem: Letter requests arrive by email with missing deadlines and no reminder of who the student is. Deadlines slip when everything lives in an inbox, and each letter starts from a blank page.
2026-10-22-3.forWhom: Faculty who write 20 or more recommendation letters a year.
benefits: A personal request link that collects what you need, including the student's consent
A deadline dashboard with reminders
Notes on each student, kept during the term
Reuse one letter across several programs

2026-10-23-1.summary: Paste in an assignment and its rubric and see how well today's AI tools would score on it, before your students try.
2026-10-23-1.problem: Instructors are told to test their assignments against AI, but doing it by hand across several tools and grading the results takes an evening per assignment. Most never do, and find out from a stack of suspiciously polished submissions.
2026-10-23-1.forWhom: Instructors and course coordinators who still set take-home writing or programming work.
benefits: Runs your assignment through several AI tools, from lazy to careful attempts
Scores each attempt against your own rubric
Re-test after you change the assignment and compare
A one-page report to share with colleagues

2026-10-23-2.summary: An honest accessibility report (VPAT) for your product, for a fraction of what an agency charges.
2026-10-23-2.problem: Universities now ask for an accessibility report before they will buy, even for small purchases. Small software companies have no accessibility staff, and agency audits cost thousands before the report is written.
2026-10-23-2.forWhom: Founders and small teams selling software to colleges and universities.
benefits: Automatic accessibility checks across your product's screens
A guided checklist for the parts a machine cannot judge
A report in the standard format that buyers ask for
Warnings before you claim something you cannot back up

2026-10-23-3.summary: Write an exam question once and print a different version for every seat, each with its own answer key.
2026-10-23-3.problem: Paper exams stop AI use but bring back copying from neighbors in crowded rooms. Writing several versions of a code-tracing exam by hand, with matching keys, takes hours and introduces mistakes in the keys.
2026-10-23-3.forWhom: Instructors and head TAs who give in-person exams in large programming courses.
benefits: Question templates that generate many versions
Answer keys checked by actually running the code
A different PDF for every seat, with a seating map
Ready to grade in Gradescope with the right key for each version

2026-10-24-1.summary: New TAs practice office hours with simulated students before they meet real ones.
2026-10-24-1.problem: New TAs face confused, stressed or upset students with no practice, so they give away answers or freeze, and the coordinator hears about it weeks later. Role-play with real people does not scale to hundreds of TAs.
2026-10-24-1.forWhom: TA coordinators and teaching faculty in departments that train many TAs each term.
benefits: A library of realistic student situations
Practice by text or voice
Feedback on giving away answers, asking good questions and calming things down
A dashboard showing who is ready and who needs coaching

2026-10-24-2.summary: Fix the technical words your lecture's automatic captions get wrong, using your own slides and code.
2026-10-24-2.problem: Automatic captions mangle technical terms, and fixing an hour of captions by hand takes an evening. Human captioning costs a dollar a minute or more.
2026-10-24-2.forWhom: Instructors in technical fields who post recorded lectures, and the staff who support them.
benefits: Learns your course's vocabulary from your slides and code
Corrects the jargon and shows you every change
Only the doubtful lines are left for a quick review
Corrected captions ready to upload again

2026-10-24-3.summary: One clear set of AI rules per assignment, and one page where students see the rules for all their courses.
2026-10-24-3.problem: Every instructor writes their own AI policy, so a student in four courses faces four different rules and worries about breaking one by accident. Teaching centers hand out templates that instructors paste in by hand.
2026-10-24-3.forWhom: Departments and teaching centers, their instructors, and their students.
benefits: Instructors pick an AI-use level for each assignment in a minute
Consistent wording and badges across the department
One page per student with the rules for every course
An overview for chairs of which policies are in use

2026-10-25-1.summary: A replacement for GitHub Classroom: create student repositories, grade them automatically and send scores straight to Canvas.
2026-10-25-1.problem: GitHub Classroom has shut down. The free replacement needs a paid GitHub organization and a risky access token, and its scores still have to be loaded into Canvas by hand every week.
2026-10-25-1.forWhom: Programming instructors and head TAs who used GitHub Classroom.
benefits: Student repositories created on any GitHub organization
Class roster from Canvas, and grades sent back to it
Automatic grading with points per test
A move-over wizard from your old GitHub Classroom setup

2026-10-25-2.summary: Accreditation paperwork from the grades you already have: rubric scores mapped to outcomes, and the tables drafted for you.
2026-10-25-2.problem: Every accreditation cycle, faculty fill in spreadsheets and one coordinator chases, merges and writes them up. The big assessment platforms need a contract and a campus rollout, so small departments stay on spreadsheets.
2026-10-25-2.forWhom: Accreditation coordinators in small and teaching-focused computing departments.
benefits: Pulls rubric scores from Canvas and Gradescope
Maps them to your program's outcomes
A dashboard that flags outcomes below target
Draft tables and an improvement log for the self-study

2026-10-25-3.summary: Turn years of student course comments into themes, fair quotes and a draft teaching reflection for your promotion file.
2026-10-25-3.problem: Promotion and tenure files now ask how you used student comments to improve your courses. Reading hundreds of comments across years and picking fair examples takes a week, usually the same month everything else is due.
2026-10-25-3.forWhom: Faculty preparing promotion, tenure or post-tenure review files.
benefits: Import comments from every course and term
See the themes and how they changed over time
Pick balanced, representative quotes
A draft reflection that fits the page limit

2026-10-26-1.summary: After your course moves to Canvas, one scan lists everything the move broke, with one-click fixes for the common problems.
2026-10-26-1.problem: When a course is copied from another system into Canvas, nobody tells you what did not survive. You click through every quiz, rubric and module looking for broken links, lost rubrics and wrong points.
2026-10-26-1.forWhom: Faculty and instructional designers moving courses into Canvas.
benefits: A prioritized list of what is broken, with links straight to it
A progress meter for 'ready for students'
Safe bulk fixes such as shifting dates
A report to review with an instructional designer

2026-10-26-2.summary: When you suspect AI misuse across a large class, build a fair, documented case for each student instead of sending a rushed mass email.
2026-10-26-2.problem: Integrity offices want the syllabus, the instructions, the student's work and meeting notes for every case, and a detector score is not enough. Building that by hand for dozens of students takes weeks, so many cases go unreported or get handled badly.
2026-10-26-2.forWhom: Instructors and head TAs of large courses who handle many suspected cases a term.
benefits: A case file per student with a checklist your campus requires
Meeting scripts and a neutral timeline
Notice letters that name the specific assignments
A referral file the integrity office will accept

2026-10-26-3.summary: Extension requests through one form, routine ones approved automatically, and new due dates set in Canvas and Gradescope for you.
2026-10-26-3.problem: Every week brings extension emails. Each one means deciding, replying, and setting a new date by hand in two systems, while a spreadsheet of who has used their free extensions keeps breaking.
2026-10-26-3.forWhom: Instructors and course staff of medium and large courses using Canvas and Gradescope.
benefits: One request page for students
Your policy approves routine requests on its own
New dates written into Canvas and Gradescope automatically
A record of each student's extensions and standing accommodations

2026-10-27-1.summary: Practice for teachers taking the computer science teaching exam, built around reading and tracing real code.
2026-10-27-1.problem: Many teachers are asked to teach a new computer science course and must pass the certification exam to keep it. The prep available is a generic study guide, which does not show why your reading of a loop was wrong.
2026-10-27-1.forWhom: Licensed teachers adding a computer science certification.
benefits: Code-reading questions that show exactly where your answer went wrong
A diagnostic of your weak areas
A weekly study plan that fits a working teacher's schedule
Timed full-length practice exams

2026-10-27-2.summary: Place dozens or hundreds of TAs in minutes instead of a week of spreadsheet juggling.
2026-10-27-2.problem: Every term brings hundreds of TA applications, instructor wish lists by email and a timetable from the registrar. Matching people to sections while checking hours and clashes takes days, and then the drops start.
2026-10-27-2.forWhom: Coordinators and associate chairs in departments that hire many TAs.
benefits: Application and instructor request forms in one place
Timetable clashes caught automatically
An assignment that respects every rule, re-done in seconds after a change
Exports for HR and roster emails

2026-10-27-3.summary: One 'join the lab' page that collects comparable answers from everyone who asks, and sends each of them a kind, honest reply.
2026-10-27-3.problem: Faculty get hundreds of cold emails asking for a research position, many clearly written by a chatbot. Ignoring them feels bad, and answering each one by hand is not sustainable.
2026-10-27-3.forWhom: Research faculty and lab managers who receive many cold inquiries.
benefits: A structured page applicants fill in instead of emailing
Inquiries grouped by position type
Automatic replies that match whether you are hiring
A quick check of who actually read your work

2026-10-28-1.summary: Test your Gradescope autograders on your own computer, against last term's submissions, before students find the broken test.
2026-10-28-1.problem: Every autograder change means uploading, waiting for it to build and checking results in a browser. With fewer TAs, a broken test means a flood of regrade requests at midnight.
2026-10-28-1.forWhom: Programming instructors and head TAs who write Gradescope autograders.
benefits: Run the autograder locally exactly as Gradescope would
Re-grade past submissions after every change and see what moved
Warnings when a test leaks hidden answers to students
Changes reviewed like any other code

2026-10-28-2.summary: A phone-friendly seat map and time-stamped notes for exam proctors, turned into a clean report for the integrity office.
2026-10-28-2.problem: When every exam must be proctored, a proctor who sees something has to report it and may be asked to testify. With a paper seating chart and memory, the details are gone by the time the report is written.
2026-10-28-2.forWhom: Faculty, TAs and staff who proctor large in-person exams, and the coordinators who organize them.
benefits: Students check in to seats, building a live seat map
One tap records what happened, when, and at which seat
An incident report with neighbors and a timeline, in your office's format
Records kept and deleted to match your policy

2026-10-28-3.summary: Track what happens to graduates of short workforce programs and produce the completion and job-placement rates funding applications ask for.
2026-10-28-3.problem: New federal funding for short job-training programs requires proof that most students finish and find jobs. Registration systems know who finished, and nothing after that, and email surveys get a handful of replies.
2026-10-28-3.forWhom: Workforce and continuing-education offices at community and technical colleges.
benefits: Import completers from your registration system
Follow-up messages at 30, 90 and 180 days by email and text
A log of employer confirmations
The completion and placement rates the application needs

2026-10-29-1.summary: Check every reference in a whole class's papers and flag the ones that do not exist or do not match.
2026-10-29-1.problem: Some references in student papers are now invented outright, and others cite real articles with the wrong details. Checking 80 bibliographies by hand takes longer than grading the papers, and a citation that does not exist holds up in an integrity case where a detector score does not.
2026-10-29-1.forWhom: Instructors and TAs who grade papers with references, in any subject.
benefits: Upload a whole assignment at once
Every reference checked against scholarly databases
Clear labels: verified, wrong details, or not found
An evidence sheet ready for the integrity office

2026-10-29-2.summary: Make your LaTeX notes and slides produce accessible PDFs: find what blocks it, fix the sources, and check the result.
2026-10-29-2.problem: Accessibility rules now cover course PDFs, but campus remediation will not touch math, and the usual PDF tools cannot fix it. Turning on LaTeX's new accessibility support breaks many templates, and you cannot tell whether the result is actually accessible.
2026-10-29-2.forWhom: Math, statistics, computing, physics and engineering faculty who write course materials in LaTeX.
benefits: A scan of what in your setup blocks accessible output
Automatic fixes to your sources, for you to review
Suggested descriptions for figures, with your approval
A checked, accessible PDF and a report for the accessibility office

2026-10-29-3.summary: Check every reference and formatting rule in your paper before you submit, and fix the bibliography in place.
2026-10-29-3.problem: Conferences now reject papers outright, and can ban every author, over a single invented reference. With several co-authors sharing one bibliography file, nobody knows who added what, and checking 80 entries the night before the deadline is not realistic.
2026-10-29-3.forWhom: Researchers and graduate students submitting to computing conferences.
benefits: Every reference checked against the authoritative sources
Corrected entries with one click
Who added each entry, from the file's history
Checks for page limits, anonymity and figure descriptions

2026-11-01-1.summary: Find the dead code embeds on your course pages and replace them with runnable code that cannot be shut down again.
2026-11-01-1.problem: Services that let you embed runnable code in course pages are shutting down, and pages now show 'no longer available' where the examples used to be. Finding and replacing every embed by hand across a site or textbook is slow.
2026-11-01-1.forWhom: Instructors, open-textbook authors and course-site maintainers with embedded code examples.
benefits: An inventory of every embedded snippet on your site
Recovered code where it can be saved
Replacements that run in the reader's browser, with nothing to shut down
A list of anything that could not be recovered

2026-11-02-1.summary: Check that your shop's cookie banner really blocks tracking until a visitor agrees, and find which plugin broke it.
2026-11-02-1.problem: You install a cookie consent plugin and assume it works. Then a routine plugin update starts tracking visitors before they choose, and nobody notices until a complaint or a demand letter arrives.
2026-11-02-1.forWhom: Owners of small online shops, and the web agencies that look after them.
benefits: A clear list of tracking that happens before consent
The plugin responsible, where it can be identified
A comparison with your last check after an update
For agencies: checks across all your client sites
